chunks.text: A derivative in an applied context is an instantaneous rate of change: how fast the output quantity changes per unit of the input quantity.
A complete interpretation of f'(a) states three things: that it is a rate of change, its units, and the meaning of its sign.
The units of a derivative are the output units divided by the input units, coming directly from the difference quotient that defines the derivative.
A positive derivative means the quantity is increasing at that instant; a negative derivative means it is decreasing; a zero derivative means it is momentarily neither rising nor falling.
If P(t) is population in thousands and t is in years, then P'(4) = 7 means that at year 4 the population is increasing at a rate of 7 thousand people per year.
The function value f(a) is an amount, while the derivative f'(a) is a rate of change; they carry different units and must not be confused.
For V(t) in liters and t in seconds, V(3) = 50 means there are 50 liters at 3 seconds, whereas V'(3) = 50 means the volume is increasing at 50 liters per second at 3 seconds.
A reliable AP interpretation template is: 'At [input value with unit], the [quantity] is increasing or decreasing at a rate of [number] [output unit] per [input unit].'
Omitting units or describing f'(a) as an amount rather than a rate loses the interpretation point on free response, even when the numerical value is correct.
For a cost function C(x) in dollars for x items, C'(x) is the marginal cost in dollars per item, approximately the cost of producing one more item.
The average rate of change of f over [a, b] is [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a), the slope of the secant line connecting the endpoints.
The instantaneous rate of change at a point is f'(a), the slope of the tangent line and the limit of average rates as the interval shrinks to zero.
Average rate of change is like average speed over a trip, while instantaneous rate is like the speedometer reading at one moment; the two can differ greatly.
When a problem says 'average rate of change,' compute a secant slope from two values; when it says 'rate of change at t = a,' compute or estimate the derivative.
To estimate a derivative f'(a) from a table, use a symmetric difference quotient with the data points on either side of a for the best accuracy.
Example: for oven temperatures T = 70, 180, 300, 340 at t = 0, 5, 10, 15, the average rate of change over [0, 15] is (340 − 70)/15 = 18 degrees per minute.
Example: from the same table, T'(10) is estimated by the symmetric difference (340 − 180)/(15 − 5) = 16 degrees per minute.
Units serve as an error detector: if a computed quantity's units do not match what the question asks for, a mistake has been made in choosing the operation.
If a rate is given in liters per minute and the question asks for total liters, integrating (not differentiating) the rate over time produces liters, because the minutes cancel.
The differential approximation Δy ≈ f'(a)·Δx is unit-consistent because f'(a) carries output-per-input units and Δx carries input units, leaving output units for Δy.
A zero derivative often marks a maximum or minimum of the quantity, since the rate of change is momentarily zero where a curve levels off.
Interpreting derivatives in context is a frequent AP free-response task that rewards a sentence containing a rate, a sign meaning, and correct units.
